Interpretation
The client's total score indicates significant dissociative experiences that exceed what is typically
observed in non-clinical adolescents. They are likely experiencing pervasive challenges across
multiple domains of dissociation that may impact their daily functioning. Their score is higher
than 99.9% of non-clinical adolescents and is consistent with levels seen in adolescents with
dissociative disorders. A comprehensive assessment for possible dissociative disorders is
recommended.
Responses to the following items contributed to the client's high score:
- 4. I can do something really well one time and then I can't do it at all another time. (9)
- 1. I get so wrapped up in watching TV, reading, or playing a video game that I don't have any
idea what's going on around me. (8)
- 2. I get back tests or homework that I don't remember doing. (8)
- 3. I have strong feelings that don't seem like they are mine. (8)
- 5. People tell me I do or say things that I don't remember doing or saying. (8)
Area(s) of Difficulty:
The responses on the Depersonalisation/Derealization subscale indicate experiences of feeling
disconnected from oneself or perceiving the world as unreal or distorted. Their score is on the
99th percentile when compared to a non-clinical adolescent sample. These experiences may
include feeling as though they are standing outside of their body, watching themselves as if they
were another person, feeling that their body does not belong to them, or perceiving familiar
environments as strange and unfamiliar. In therapy, grounding techniques and skills to enhance
present-moment awareness and connection to physical sensations may be beneficial for
reducing these symptoms.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 3. I have strong feelings that don't seem like they are mine. (8)
- 11. I am so good at lying and acting that I believe it myself. (8)
- 6. I feel like I am in a fog or spaced out and things around me seem unreal. (7)

Interpretation (cont.)
The responses on the Passive Influence subscale reflect experiences of not feeling in control of
one's actions, behaviours, or emotions. Their score is on the 99th percentile when compared to
a non-clinical adolescent sample. The client may report feeling that something inside of them
seems to make them do things that they don't want to do, or that they can do something really
well one time and then can't do it at all another time. These experiences can be disorienting and
distressing. Therapeutic approaches might include enhancing the client's sense of agency and
control, exploring potential triggers, and developing self-regulation skills.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 4. I can do something really well one time and then I can't do it at all another time. (9)
- 14. I find myself going somewhere or doing something and I don't know why. (6)
- 19. I find myself doing something that I know is wrong, even when I really don’t want to do it.
The responses on the Absorption subscale indicate a tendency to become highly engrossed in
activities or fantasy to the point of reduced awareness of surroundings. Their score is on the
99th percentile when compared to a non-clinical adolescent sample. While some absorption can
be adaptive and is common in adolescence, high levels may indicate using absorption as a
coping mechanism to avoid distress. In therapy, developing awareness of when this occurs and
expanding their repertoire of coping strategies may be helpful. Mindfulness techniques could
assist in maintaining present-moment awareness.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 1. I get so wrapped up in watching TV, reading, or playing a video game that I don't have any
idea what's going on around me. (8)
- 7. I get confused about whether I have dones something or only thought about doing it. (8)
- 10. When I am somewhere that I don't want to be, I can go away in my mind. (7)
The responses on the Amnesia subscale indicate difficulties with memory gaps and forgetting
important personal information or events. Their score is on the 99th percentile when compared
to a non-clinical adolescent sample. These experiences may involve finding unfamiliar items
among personal belongings, being told about doing things they don't remember, or having gaps
in awareness while performing activities. In therapy, exploration of these memory disruptions
may be important, particularly in the context of any reported trauma history. Grounding
techniques and strategies to improve present-moment awareness may be beneficial.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 2. I get back tests or homework that I don't remember doing. (8)
- 5. People tell me I do or say things that I don't remember doing or saying. (8)
- 8. I look at the clock and realize that time has gone by and I can't remember what has
happened. (7)
Scoring and Interpretation Information
The A-DES is scored by calculating the mean of all 30 items, resulting in a total score ranging
from 0 to 10. Higher scores indicate greater frequency and severity of dissociative experiences.

Scoring and Interpretation Information (cont.)
The four A-DES subscale scores can be calculated to provide a more nuanced understanding of
the adolescent's dissociative experiences:
Dissociative amnesia (items: 2, 5, 8, 12, 15, 22, 27): assesses gaps in memory and awareness.
Absorption and imaginative involvement (items 1, 7, 10, 18, 24, 28): measures the tendency to
become highly engrossed in activities with reduced awareness of surroundings.
Passive influence (items 4, 14, 16, 19, 23): examines experiences of not having volitional control
over one's body and sensations.
Depersonalisation and derealization (items 3, 6, 9, 11, 13, 17, 20, 21, 25, 26, 29, 30): reflects
feelings of disconnection from one's body and the world.
NovoPsych have created the following guidelines to assist in interpretation:
Low (0-1.9): Minimal dissociative experiences; typical of non-clinical adolescents.
Mild (2.0-2.9): Some dissociative experiences but generally within normal limits for adolescents.
Moderate (3.0-3.9): Notable dissociative experiences that may indicate elevated risk.
High (4.0 and above): Significant dissociative experiences consistent with clinical levels.
The total score is often expressed as a percentile rank based on normative data from non-
clinical adolescent samples. This percentile contextualises the adolescent's score relative to
peers, indicating the percentage of adolescents who scored lower. For example, a score at the
85th percentile means that 85% of adolescents in the normative sample scored lower, placing
the individual in the upper range of dissociative experiences.
On first administration a stacked bar graph showing total and subscale average scores is
displayed, along with a comparison graph illustrating the client's scores relative to different
reference groups. When the assessment is administered multiple times, longitudinal line graphs
are generated to track changes in both total and subscale average scores over time.
When tracking clinical progress, a meaningful change is defined as an increase or decrease of
at least half a standard deviation in the total score (approximately .9 points on the 0-10 scale)
This criterion is based on the Minimally Important Difference (MID) calculation (Turner et al.,
2010). Such changes indicate meaningful improvement or reduction in symptoms, while a
change of less than the specified points suggests no meaningful change in symptom severity
between assessments. Regular monitoring of A-DES scores can help evaluate treatment
effectiveness and guide intervention.
